name: DivineTV
tagline: A subscription streaming service for faith-based films, documentaries and series.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The app here is a video player with a search box and a billing wall, and yes, an agent can build that before lunch. The product is the catalog: licensed films, documentaries and series that someone negotiated, paid for and is allowed to stream to you. Nothing you write produces a single minute of that footage, and pointing your clone at pirated copies is a different hobby with different consequences. The closest honest personal version is a media server for things you already own, which is a solved problem with better existing options than whatever you ship tonight. Build it if you want a tidy shelf for your own files, not if you want their shelf.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted web player that indexes video files you already own, shows them in a browsable grid, and remembers where you stopped watching.
requirements: Video files you actually own or have rights to
A machine that stays on, or a cheap VPS with enough disk
ffmpeg installed for thumbnails and metadata
whatYouLose: The entire licensed catalog, which is the whole reason anyone subscribes
Apps on TV platforms: Roku, Fire TV, Apple TV, Android TV
Adaptive bitrate streaming and a CDN that does not choke on your home upload
New releases, curation and whatever the service adds next month
Offline downloads and cross-device resume that actually works
moatNotes: Licensing is the product. The frontend is a commodity and everyone in streaming knows it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because they want to watch specific films they cannot otherwise get, on a TV, without thinking about transcoding profiles. A niche catalog is worth paying for precisely because it is niche: nobody else assembled it, and the rights holders are scattered enough that nobody casually will. Add the family-friendly curation angle and the subscription is buying a decision filter, not a video player. You cannot code your way into a licensing deal.
notes: The player is a one-sitting build; the catalog is a legal department. The moat is content rights, plus TV-platform distribution that takes months of certification per device.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted personal video library and web player for video files I already own. Single user, runs on my own machine, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Node 20, TypeScript, Fastify for the server, SQLite via better-sqlite3 for the index, plain server-rendered HTML with a little vanilla JS. No React, no Next, no Docker, no auth provider.

In scope:
- Read a MEDIA_DIR path from .env and recursively scan it for .mp4, .mkv, .webm, .mov on startup and on a /rescan endpoint.
- For each file store path, size, duration, and an optional sidecar .json for title, year, description, tags. Parse the filename as a fallback title.
- Generate one poster thumbnail per file with ffmpeg at the 10 percent mark, cache it in a .thumbs folder, serve it.
- Library page: responsive poster grid, search box filtering on title and tags, tag filter chips, sort by title or date added.
- Detail page: poster, metadata, play button.
- Player page: native HTML5 video element, HTTP Range requests supported properly so seeking works, keyboard shortcuts for space, arrows, f for fullscreen.
- Resume: store playback position in SQLite every 10 seconds, show a progress bar on the poster, resume from last position with a 5 second rewind.
- A "Continue watching" row at the top of the library.
- Serve .srt and .vtt subtitle sidecars as a video track, converting srt to vtt on the fly.

Out of scope, do not build: transcoding, user accounts, payments, any content discovery or download feature, any scraper that pulls media from the internet, TV apps, mobile apps.

Deliver: a README with setup steps, an .env.example with MEDIA_DIR and PORT, and `npm run dev` working on first try. Fail loudly with a clear message if ffmpeg is missing or MEDIA_DIR does not exist.
